utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution. The Prosecution is represented by just one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Ekkehard Withopf and Kimberly Fleming as the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the Defence, who are all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, and I'm assisted by my co-counsel, Stephane Bourgon for General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Fahrudin Ibrisimovic. I'm assisted by Mr. Dixon and Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good day to everyone, to the accused, the Prosecution, the Defence, the administrative personnel and the interpreters. We are going to continue and we will hear a witness. If there are no comments to make at the moment, we'll bring this witness into the courtroom. Could the usher please bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good day, Witness. Can you hear me? Can you hear the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is going to continue with its examination-in-chief. The Prosecution may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Withopf: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rados. Mr. Rados, yesterday, prior to the break, I was about to finish my examination. There are only a few questions left. Prior to the break, you were telling the Trial Chamber about your treatment in the Zenica Music School. And to summarise your last sentences, you were telling the Trial Chamber that you were kicked, that you were hit in the rib area with a wooden object which looked like a baseball bat, and that they started hitting you with that bat in the rib area and they stopped when they heard a loud noise. Mr. Rados, can you tell the Trial Chamber what this loud noise was about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could hear something, as if something had broken. After that, they stopped. Someone just kicked me once more. That was someone who was wearing trainers, and he stopped after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could hear something was broken. What was broken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a sharp -- I felt a sharp pain in the ribs. When they left, it was difficult for me to walk. The pain was excruciating. It was difficult for me to breathe. I had to breathe in slowly. A few days later - I don't know how long we were there for; two, three, or four days - we were transferred to the Zenica KPD, correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you here, Mr. Rados. You were telling the Trial Chamber that you have been beaten by two individuals. Do you know or did you get to know who has beaten you in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I'd never seen those two men. I wasn't even able to see the face of one of them. But I heard that the one who was shorter, I heard that his name was Geler. This is what I heard later on. I don't know when; perhaps after we had left the Zenica KPD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long, Mr. Rados, have you been detained in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many days we were detained there exactly, but three or four days. Between two and five days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you brought to once you left the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken from the Zenica Music School to the Zenica KPD in a van. They first took us to -- into some of the offices in the KPD. I can't remember who was there exactly now, but they were different from -- they were quite different from the people in the first building. They were more friendly, and someone told us who had been killed in the Lasva local commune, in the area where conflict had broken out. Afterwards, they transferred us with the others who had been brought in from Lasva, and we remained together until the end. In the Zenica KPD, we were treated very differently than in the other building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our treatment was far better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the Zenica Music School, what language was spoken by the guards in the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language spoken in the music school in Zenica was the language that was spoken in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, the same language that I speak. But the last time I was interviewed -- the last time I was questioned up there, there was someone who spoke our original language, but he would sing after the questioning. He would start singing. He would sing various songs, and I noticed that these were sung in the Arab language. He did that perfectly. And later, as far as I know, someone asked him -- it seemed that he was a quite literate man, an educated man, in view of the way that he spoke. I remember his educational background, and I remember him saying that he had graduated from some sort of special school. And we didn't speak about that matter any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Rados.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Defence takes the floor, there is a matter of clarification. I would like to ask you something about -- that concerns your examination-in-chief yesterday. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the -- to Zvonko Radic's attempt to flee and what happened after that. Could you tell me, to the extent that you remember this, when he fled, according to what you said, I think someone shot at him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you then noticed that he had been wounded as a result of this shot.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After he had been wounded, what did you see? What did you see or what did you hear? Did the wounded person say anything or not, and what did you see afterwards? What did you personally see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was groaning. It was probably because of the pain. I couldn't see him because of the position I was in and because of his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you realise that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was first of all wounded, and then some of our soldiers carried him. We took him back to Kruska. We carried him. That was near my old house. We put him down there to have a rest. And from the opposite direction there were several BH army members who came to him. They ran up to him. As soon as they arrived, they started kicking him. I don't know how long this lasted. It wasn't very long. One of the BH army soldiers had a short-barrelled automatic weapon, and he fired a shot in the upper area of the chest. It was near the neck, somewhere in this area. And after that, he stopped groaning. You couldn't hear him any more. He was probably dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you said that when you put him down near the pear tree he was still alive. When he was put down there, he was still alive.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I don't think I put him down at the time. We would change. All I know is that he was put down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. The Defence may now take the floor and commence its cross-examination. The Trial Chamber would prefer to ask questions, to enable the Defence to see if there is any -- if there are any ambiguities. I think it is better than if the Trial Chamber intervenes and asks questions after the examination and the cross-examination have been completed. You may take the floor now. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Rados.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I would like to ask you a few questions. Before your testimony here, you gave a statement to the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement you also spoke about the general situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I ask you a number of questions, since you are familiar with the situation in the place where you were located, I will also ask you some general questions. So I would be grateful if you could tell me what you know. You lived in the hamlet of Brdo, which belongs to the Lasva municipality, and Lasva was part of the municipality of Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Lasva - that is to say, from the railway station in Lasva - up to the Brdo hamlet, which is where you lived, the distance is about 1 and a half kilometres, and up to Dusina the distance is about 2 and a half kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so. It depends on the part of the village of Dusina that you were thinking of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But the hamlet could be -- the hamlets could be at a distance of 500 metres perhaps, something like that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the lie of the land - and I think the Trial Chamber has heard something about this already - from the position where your house was located, you weren't able to see the hamlet of Kegelj which was in the valley, and you weren't able to hear what was happening there either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the same reason, from the position of your house in the village of Brdo, you weren't able to see or hear what was happening in the village of Lasva, in the vicinity -- in the area around the railway station.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I could hear anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a question from my learned colleague, you yesterday said that in 1991 you were a member of the HVO and you were also the leader of a squad in Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO commander for Lasva and the president of the HDZ in that area was Zvonko Rajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you belonged to the Zenica municipality, your superior command wasn't the Jure Francetic Brigade, with its headquarters in Zenica. You belonged to the command in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our unit, the HVO Lasva Unit, and we were the HVO in Central Bosnia. I still don't understand how these commands work, but I know that Zvonko Rajic had some connection with Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your unit in Lasva also received some weapons from Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had mostly light automatic weapons. Only Zeljko Cvijanovic had an Austria sniper, an Austrian Winchester; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had light infantry weapons, but I don't know who -- I'm not certain who had the sniper. Perhaps he did; perhaps someone else had the sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous statement - and I am now asking you about this so that we can hear your answer before the Trial Chamber - you said that in the middle of January the situation in Busovaca became more complex and an open conflict between the HVO and the army broke out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And refugees started arriving in the area of Lasva, Muslim women and children, and they would say what was happening. They would have stories about what was happening there; is that correct ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That made the situation in your local commune more complicated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO held a checkpoint in Lasva. They had a checkpoint there. And they would control the road from the junction to the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a checkpoint in Lasva. As for the control of the road -- well, I couldn't say that they controlled the road. The checkpoint was there to guard the bridge, the railway, the shop, the post office, the railway tracks and the medical institute. That was the purpose of the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before these events that you have testified about, there was an attack carried out against the village of Merdani and you could hear artillery shelling in Lasva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of the danger, and on several occasions there was a meeting with representatives of the army. And a day or two before the conflict, on the premises of the local commune, a meeting was held which you attended too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how much in advance, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, Zvonko Rajic, Ivica Filipovic, and Ante Kristo, Zeljko Cvijanovic as HVO representatives, in addition to yourself also attended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who was there exactly, but Zvonko Rajic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From representatives of the BH army and because the HVO units were in an open conflict with the army, several suggestions were made: Either that your unit should join the HVO brigade in Zenica or the entire village should be disarmed or you should be subordinated to the army or you should move to the Busovaca area. Were these suggestions discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in the area of the confluence of the Lasva and Bosna River, the BH army troops started massing there. Two or three days or perhaps a week earlier, a week before the conflict broke out in the Busovaca area -- well, this meeting was held in the local commune. I can't remember whether it was two, three, or four days before, because the conflict hadn't broken out in Busovaca when the meeting was held. And members of the BH army attended the meeting, and one could say that some HVO Lasva members attended it too. And at that meeting the HVO discussed the subject of the local commune of Lasva and the people in the local commune. They said they should stand -- they should stand outside the conflict, they should not be in the conflict, and that the problems between the BH army in Lasva and the HVO in Lasva should be solved. It was said that we shouldn't join Busovaca or Zenica or any other conflict. It was said that the problems should be solved in Lasva. And the people who came to the confluence of the Lasva and Bosna River, in that area, it was said that they weren't from the area that we lived in and that they were a potential danger for the Croats in Lasva and that they shouldn't be there and that the BH army could solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that in the afternoon on the 25th of January the HVO arrested, disarmed, and brought in two members of the BH army from Dusina -- in Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrested them, brought them in -- well, I couldn't say so. After that meeting - I can't remember everything very well - but I know that the HVO tried to do everything to avoid getting involved in the events unfolding in Busovaca and to avoid going to Busovaca and to ensure that the BH army didn't go to that part. Two BH army members from that local commune, as far as I know, came from the direction of Busovaca. They were detained between 15 and 20 minutes, and Zvonko Rajic was informed that he should phone Hazim Barucija and that the president of the BH army -- the representative of the BH army and to have a meeting in order to solve that problem, to avoid a conflict in the place where we lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your insistence, after a certain period of time, these people were released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I released them. I apologised to them. I didn't -- release them, but we couldn't find Hazim Barucija to tell him that they went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We apologised, gave them their weapons, and told them that for security reasons they shouldn't go to Lasva. We allowed them to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on that same day, in the afternoon, your family left Brdo and went to Dusina and found accommodation in the Kegelj settlement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That afternoon, the families of Zvonko Rajic and some other HVO members from Lasva and Donja Visnjica also went there and found accommodation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that my family was there, but I only found out that all the others were there a lot later. The reason for which my wife and son went there is there was an event a week earlier, perhaps even more than that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not go into what happened before.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I should explain this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you think so, please go ahead, but I'd appreciate it if you could answer the questions that I ask you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A week or ten days earlier I wasn't at home. Someone came to the door of my house, knocked on the door. Only my wife and son were inside. My wife asked, "Who is it? Who is it," and no one answered. But the knocking continued. It was dark. She took the rifle that I had and said to the person that the person should stop or she would shoot. I don't know how long the knocking continued, but afterwards she fired a few shots at the door and I think that after that she stayed there every night, because she couldn't remain in the house. I don't know exactly, but I know that she was stressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Mr. Rados, in your earlier statement, you said that these families -- I'm paraphrasing your statement. Can you please follow me closely -- that these families were placed in Kegelj because this was closest to Busovaca, because everybody was withdrawing to Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan for the withdrawal of the Croatian people in Lasva was drafted I believe while the Serbs were still down there, and this is the only plan that was drafted in case we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move to 26 January. In the early morning hours, you heard gunfire, and you said that it came from all directions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you came out of the house, the troops were in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As soon as you left the house, you surrendered your weapons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as soon as I left the house. When I came to my old house, I found a bigger group of soldiers there, and that's where I surrendered my weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that moment, you saw this dead soldier, Nedin Cavcic [phoen], a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his name was, and at that moment I wasn't aware of the fact that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After -- above your house on Brdo there was an HVO group which participated in the combat activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO group was across from the BH army on a -- on the opposite hilltop, between Brdo and Donja Visnjica, and the place is called Brnjici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not for a single moment did you join this group and participate in combat activities against the members of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. After I surrendered my weapons, I joined the negotiations. I went there with my wife, and then I spoke to Edin Hakanovic. I don't know on how many occasions. Two or three occasions, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your only mission was to be mediator, together with your wife, between the BH army and representatives of the HVO who were on their positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up there you saw Zvonko Rajic as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up there you didn't see Zeljko Cvijanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Zvonko Rajic. I know that because I spoke to him. And the only person I can remember now is him. I don't think that I saw the other person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in Busovaca, immediately after you were released from the KPD in February 1993, you gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was such a statement, it wouldn't be yours then; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to show this statement to the witness. I would like him to tell us whether this is his signature. I would like to ask him a few questions. Although I'm not tendering this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections from the OTP, Madam Usher -- Or maybe we do have an objection on the part of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There's no objection. However, the Prosecution would like to get a copy prior to questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, take the document and show it to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement is in Croatian. And I just wanted to show it to the witness in order for him to recognise his signature. The source is the HV archives in Zagreb. Since we are not tendering the document, we didn't think it was necessary for it to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution objects. We only got a copy of a statement in the B/C/S language, and we are not in a position to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is that the document is in B/C/S, but the only thing that you want confirmed is the signature. In that case, you can present the document to the witness just to see whether this is his signature, if that is your only objective. Madam Usher, you can show the witness the document, and we can then ask him whether this indeed is his signature. So he is not going to read the contents of the document; he is just going to see whether the signature on the document is his. Witness, now you have the document in front of you. Can you please confirm for us that this is your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may now return the document to the Defence. You may pursue your line of questioning. If you want to tender this document, then you have to have it translated and -- otherwise, we would not be able to know the contents of it. I know that you've had difficulties with translation. And as I've already indicated, if you want to tender a document, you have to address the Registry, and this document will then be translated for you for the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have already sent some of the documents for translation, all the documents that concern Dusina. However, we have not been able to receive any translations. I'm using very few documents because I have not had them translated. Thank you very much. In any case, we are going to follow your previous instruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having looked at the statement that was given to the security service of the HVO in Busovaca, did this refresh your memory? Are you now aware of the fact that you did give a statement to the service and signed it yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember as we left the KPD all the soldiers who were HVO members, who came from the first building in the KPD, they were under a lot of stress, and I really don't remember whether I gave a statement or not. I cannot remember that this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then. In any case, if it says somewhere in this document or elsewhere that you were in the basement of your house in Brdo village, together with five other fighters, that you returned fire, and that the combat lasted for about five hours, that you were very well sheltered. That wouldn't be correct; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this question. My learned colleague is referring to in document in saying "then in any case if it says somewhere in this document or elsewhere." I object to the use of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Can you please rephrase your question, maybe not directly -- or maybe the Chamber can ask the question on your behalf. To do it on your behalf: What we are saying, when you were liberated, as you said, did you give a statement to a service, to the HVO? Did they ask you for some clarifications about the things that you had done before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't remember. I really don't know. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, you are denying that in the basement of your house there were five HVO members who opened fire on members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house does not have a basement. And I could not have been in the basement of my house with five HVO soldiers. This house simply does not have a basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your house there were negotiations between Hakanovic, yourself, and a member of the army, Zvonko Rajic, and another member of the HVO, and that's all that took place in your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my house, yes, there were negotiations between one BH army soldier, Edin Hakanovic, Zvonko Rajic, myself, and I can't remember whether there was anybody else or not. In any case, Zvonko Rajic and the ABiH soldier were the ones who talked, who were negotiating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rajic, you testified yesterday that you were disarmed after having received the news that there was an HVO ambush in Donja Visnjica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Rados. I really do apologise. Did you say that yesterday? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't concentrating on your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat. Yesterday you said that you went with the army for a certain part of the road, and after that information reached us that there was an ambush, and only after that you were disarmed. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that after Zvonko Rajic had attempted to escape and after his death, it was only then that you were tied. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier this morning to the Prosecutor's question you answered that you had been transferred to the Zenica KPD and that you were treated differently there, that the treatment was much better. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The security there was provided by the military police of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who provided security, but in any case it was the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Rados, I -- once again, I apologise for having addressed you with a different name. And I would like to thank you for having answered my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank you. And I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence of Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There are no questions on behalf of Mr. Kubura for this witness, as his testimony concerns events before the 1st of April, from the time when Mr. Kubura is not charged with any offences. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any re-examination on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's only one issue I wish to clarify. Re-examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the cross-examination by my learned colleague, there is a word missing in the transcript, and I wish the witness to clarify it. It says "Because of the lie of the land, and I think the Trial Chamber has heard something about this already, from the position you were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the interpreters cannot hear the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says in the transcript at the beginning of the cross-examination - and it's a question by my learned colleague - "Because of the lie of the land - and I think the Trial Chamber has heard something about this already - from the position where your house was located, you weren't able to see the hamlet of -- which was in the valley," and "the hamlet of" is unfortunately not detailed in the transcript. What hamlet is the witness referring to, or what hamlet is Defence counsel referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence mentioned the hamlet of Kegelj, and I believe that I received the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rados, is it correct that you couldn't see the hamlet of Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the house where I was? Is that your question? From the house where I was, my house, whether I could see that hamlet?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the position you have been at the time, at your house.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN RADOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: There are no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination are over. We have had some re-examination, so we may now state that this witness's testimony is over. We would like to thank you for having come from so far. We wish you a happy journey back home. I would kindly ask the usher to take you out of the courtroom. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I be allowed to say something before I leave the courtroom, please? Generations and generations of people have created good relationships in the local commune of Lasva, and the relationship was perfect. The relationship between people before the war were perfect, and that is the picture that I carry with me of the place where I was born. I'm trying to remember, whatever happened afterwards, I believe that the people should continue living like they lived before the war. Conditions of life of Muslims, Croats, and Serbs there were perfect, and I wish this to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have recorded what you have just said. Once again, we would like to thank you. And the usher is going to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall continue with our session. It is ten to 10.00 now. We are going to have our break at half past 10.00. The Prosecution is now going to bring in their new witness. Therefore, we are going to see a new witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution calls Franjo Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution. You are going to give me your name and your last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Franjo Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on 13 November 1935 in Dubravica, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a Franciscan priest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where do you currently serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Nova Bila. I am the head priest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You are going to take the solemn oath by reading the sentence from the piece of paper that the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. You may be seated. As you have already been told, you are going to first answer some questions put to you by the Prosecution. After that, the Defence counsel are going to ask you some questions. The Chamber also has the right to ask you questions at any moment. We have 35 minutes before the break. I'm giving the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber the assignments that you have had with the church since the time of your ordination.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: After I graduated in Sarajevo and Ljubljana, I was a chaplain in Surkovac near Ljubina, near western Bosnia. Then I was a chaplain in BH, in western Bosnia. After that, I was a priest in Dolac, Srebrena Bosna. After that, I was a member of the seniority of the Bosna Srebrena in Sarajevo for a long time. I remained in Sarajevo until 1985. I discharged various functions. I am the guardian of the monastery in Bistrik. In 1985, I became guardian -- Franciscan monastery in Guca Gora near Travnik. I served there two terms of offices until 1991. In 1991, I was transferred to a new duty of the parish priest in Brajkovici, where I remained until 1994. Then I was again appointed the guardian, and I took over the monastery in Guca Gora. This was in 1994 up until the year 2000. In the year 2000, I was transferred to a new duty, as a chaplain in Nova Bila, and this is where I am working today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, witness, the approximately geographic area that is covered by the Brajkovici parish at the time you were there, from 1991 through 1994.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I was appointed parish priest to work in a parish with 5.500 people. It is located in the area with the diameter of some 20 kilometres, if not more. It is, for its most part, in the territory of Travnik municipality; 20 per cent of its territory is in the territory of Zenica municipality. I worked as a priest there. I had an assistant, a chaplain, Pero Karajica. There were two nuns who worked in the parish. And at that time, I worked as a priest in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which or what were the largest -- what were the largest Croat villages that fell under the Brajkovici parish?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, the village of Brajkovici itself, which is where the centre of the parish is; then Grahovcici is the largest village; then Cukle, Gornja and Donja, Donja Cukle; then Podovi; Rudnik; Bila; and Vrbice; the village of Miletici, which is furthest from the centre of the parish. In a north-easterly direction, it's about 10 kilometres away. That's in the municipality of Travnik. But in the Zenica municipality, there's Ovnak - that's the border of the Zenica municipality - and beyond that border there's the village of Susanj and the village of Konjevici. They belong to the Brajkovici parish, as they were Croatian Catholic villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, within the area covered by the Brajkovici parish, what other ethnic groups lived in that area?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: In the area of the Brajkovici parish, there were Catholics and Muslims, and to a minor extent in the territory of the parish there was a village where there were Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the relations between the various ethnic groups living in the Brajkovici parish in 1992.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Brajkovici, I didn't notice any tension among the ethnic groups, apart from the fact that we had already heard about the war in Croatia and people were concerned on this account. In the course of 1992, some sort of shelling had started in Bosnia. Serbian units and the army had started shelling in that area. So Vitez and Busovaca were shelled. And in the territory of my parish, there were no incidents in the course of 1992. They were in fact concerned -- in fact, the Croats and the Muslims were concerned about their personal security, and they tried to cooperate, form some sort of defence for that area. So I know that in 1992, the Croats and the Muslims, acting together, a group of them, went to the Vlasic mountain, where they tried to take the television transmitter for the needs of the population, but the Serbian army was already there and they used their weapons to prevent them from taking that tower. And a parishioner of mine, Ivica Tomic, died there. He was a Croat. And someone from my village - I think it was -- Siljak was his last name. He was seriously wounded. I don't remember his first name. Unfortunately, he later succumbed to his wounds. So at that time in 1992 - at least in the first half of 1992 - there were no conflicts between the Muslims and Croats, as far as I am aware. But barricades had already been erected around the area. Everyone wanted to protect themselves. They didn't want to be attacked. They wanted to avoid anything misfortunate happening to them. In 1992, in the first half of that year, the people from those areas went to safer areas. So I know that some buses would take children towards Croatia, towards Dalmatia. And then in the second half of that year, those barricades that had been erected for the sake of security were often the cause of incidents. People would be stopped. Everyone would be stopped in front of their villages, both Croats and Bosniaks. And in the second half of 1992, foreigners also started appearing. They would speak foreign languages. They looked different. And they didn't relate to the inhabitants in the same way as the locals did, since the locals -- well, they knew each other. They were neighbours. They'd been neighbours for many years. And in Bosnia, there was a tradition of tolerance. When these foreigners appeared, various incidents started occurring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I could stop you there. You've -- you've mentioned foreigners. Do you have any idea where these foreigners came from or which foreign languages they spoke?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: There were many foreigners, and many foreign languages were spoken. But in this area, when I said "foreigners," I was referring specifically to people who had come from Arab countries. We all called them Mujahedins. I know there were people from Jordan, from Iran, from some of those countries. But I would always recognise them, because their appearance, the clothes they wore, the fact that they had long beards, and the fact that they spoke the Arab language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the approximate month when you first -- month and year when you first saw these people in the area of your parish.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I certainly saw them in the course of 1992, and I'm sure that I saw them in spring or summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the specific area or areas within the Brajkovici parish where you saw these people?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I remember I saw them in Han Bila, in Mehorce [phoen] in particular. Sometimes they would drive by. They would use the roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that in the first part of 1992 relations between the Croats and Muslims were relatively cooperative. Did there come a time when that situation changed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, at the end of 1992, that situation changed because people from both sides were stopped at the barricades and certain incidents started occurring. A vehicle would be confiscated or someone would be prevented from passing through. Such things started happening. And I remember that in 1992, when I was returning from Zenica, from the parish of St. Ilija in Zenica - that was on the 20th of July - I remember that that was the first time I came across a large column of soldiers in camouflage uniforms. They were marching in single file, from Zenica towards the west. I was supposed to visit my brother in Vitez on that occasion, so I went behind that column for a certain time. And at the periphery of Zenica, towards the north-west, they headed off towards the village of Brajkovici; and I turned to the left, in the direction of Vitez, in order to visit my brother. But I was concerned. It was something that surprised me a lot. I briefly visited my brother and hurried on towards Brajkovici. I went to see whether there was any news. When I got there, people told me that that column of soldiers in camouflage uniforms had reached the limit of the municipality of Zenica. They had reached Ovnak, the barricades that had been erected by the inhabitants of Ovnak and the surrounding villages. They got there, and there were discussions -- or there weren't any discussions, but they then returned to Zenica. So the people took this to be some sort of a threat, a challenge, a reason for concern. So that was in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know which army these soldiers were members of?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, it was the Muslim army. They were wearing green berets and camouflage uniforms, and this is the sort of uniform that that army later wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, approximately how far from Brajkovici is Ovnak?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It's about a kilometre and a half or 2 kilometres from the church in Brajkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time in early 1993 where the situation between the Muslim and Croat inhabitants of the Brajkovici parish area deteriorated even further?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, it was in 1993 when you could hear shooting, especially at night, and this wartime psychosis was beginning to spread. People were becoming increasingly afraid. And in 1993, at the beginning of that year, there were rumours of various crimes that had been committed here and there. In my parish, I was not in a position to communicate with areas beyond its territory in 1993. There was something that was particularly difficult for me. That was on the 18th of April, the first half of 1993. A real war had broken out in Zenica. You could hear shots being fired from light and heavy weapons. And afterwards there was an exodus of a lot of Croats, a lot of Catholics in this area of my parish. There were perhaps about 2.000 people who came to the village of Grahovcici. And that's when real trouble started with those people, as far as food and everything else is concerned. The area had been sealed off already, blocked. It wasn't possible to establish communications. And shortly afterwards we heard that people had been killed in the village of Miletici, which I said is to the north-west of the church in Brajkovici. We waited. We listened to people on a daily basis to find out news. And finally we really found out that people had been killed, and perhaps a week later UNPROFOR brought those people to the church in Brajkovici so that we could bury them. Those were the worst incidents, and it was a real wartime situation at that time. I tried to get food. That was at the time of Easter. I wasn't able to, so I tried to find at opportunity. I thought that these were unfortunate events, that it wasn't a real war yet, so I wanted to get food, because people didn't have sufficient supplies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned hearing that people had been killed in the village of Miletici. Do you recall who told you that and the approximate date when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Immediately after the date I mentioned. I think I heard this over the phone from the monastery in Guca Gora, which is not far from the church in Brajkovici. And I heard from my parishioners. They told me about these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, Witness, that UNPROFOR brought these people to the church for purposes of burial. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber how that came about.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I don't know who informed us exactly. Their relatives tried to obtain this, more than we did. We were told that on a certain day these dead people would be brought to Brajkovici for the purposes of burial. This is what happened. It was either a week or eight days or ten days later - I don't know exactly - UNPROFOR transported the bodies of these people in their vehicles and they brought them to the church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you have the opportunity to observe the bodies that UNPROFOR brought to the church for burial?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. As a priest, it was up to me to perform the burial rites. At the time, it was only possible for them to be buried in Grahovcici, for security reasons, and that's where most people were located, and their family members also wanted them to be buried in that cemetery; although, that cemetery did not belong to the village of Miletici. When we got to the cemetery -- when we reached the cemetery in Grahovcici in those UNPROFOR vehicles, the family members wanted the coffins to be opened so that they could see and identify the bodies. And when this was done, when the coffins were opened, I was able to see the people who had been killed. I was able to see the condition they were in, although I didn't want this episode to last very long and I wanted to perform the rites. There were a lot of people from Zenica and from other villages who had come to Grahovcici, so a lot of people were present. I was able to see those people. On the whole, they only revealed their heads. I could see that they had been covered in blood, they had been wounded, that they had knife wounds to the neck, they had haematomas on their heads, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall how many bodies you saw or how many bodies you buried from Miletici on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I saw them bury five bodies on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise any of the bodies that you buried that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Perhaps ten days before that incident I visited the village of Miletici, in order to prepare the parishioners, because there were about 15 houses far from the parish and they were surrounded by Muslim villages. I had to go there to prepare them for Easter. I had a mass there. I sat down with those people, spoke to them, et cetera. I was acquainted with them; I didn't have that much contact with any of them, because of the distance. But I did see all those people and I did know some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- you told us earlier that the family members wanted the coffins opened. Do you know who these family members were?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, the surnames were Pavlovic, Petrovic. Those were the names on the whole of the dead people, Petrovic, Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know where these family members were from?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: There were people from Miletici who had come there via the village, had come to the Grahovcici area, and there were relatives of theirs from other villages who were related to them, either through marriage or in some other way. But on the whole, it was from the area of the Brajkovici parish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that they were buried in Grahovcici. How far is Grahovcici from Brajkovici and the church in Brajkovici?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It's between a kilometre and a half to 2 kilometres. That's how the village spreads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why these five people were buried in Grahovcici.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, the area had in fact been blocked off, so people from the parish were not able to go to the village of Miletici or to Bila or to Vitez, to the south or to the north. The area had been blocked off and it wasn't safe to go anywhere; that's why we couldn't go to visit those relatives in Miletici, because all these people had already fled from Miletici. No one else could take charge of those bodies. UNPROFOR had to do it. And because of the insecurity and the situation at that time, they brought the bodies in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, while you were living in Brajkovici, did that village ever come under direct military attack?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: As I've already said, at the beginning of 1993 and afterwards, you would hear shooting at night and during the day. But on the 8th of June, 1993, that's when the real war broke out in that village area, when the village was attacked and light and heavy weapons were used. It was attacked from the east, the north, the west. It was completely surrounded. And not just the village of Brajkovici, but Grahovcici, Cukle, the core area of the parish. That was the tragic day for the parish of Brajkovici. It started in the early morning hours, and by 11.00 the situation had come to a head. People were gathering in a forest near Rudnik. There was a mass of them. I didn't know where they intended to go. Later, the people who were fleeing said that they were going there, that they were going to gather there, and that they were going to attempt to break through to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that the attack began early on the day of 8 June 1993. Do you have a recollection of the approximate time on that morning?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: We spent that morning awake more than asleep, because of the explosions. All I know is that before dawn broke, we went to the windows. We looked around. And in the early morning hours, we noticed that there were fires -- that there were houses on fire towards the village of Guca Gora; that's the Radonjici village, which you can see from the church in Brajkovici. And a little later, at about 9.00 perhaps, I could see column of people who from the monastery in Guca Gora, which is to the west of Brajkovici, had set off in the direction of Nova Bila, by Kosovo. That's the route they'd taken. It was some sort of a village road. And this was a sign that the situation was bad, and our parish was affected by it also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, where were you when you came to the realisation that Brajkovici and the surrounding area was under attack?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I was in the parish office, in the parish house in Brajkovici throughout that period, not just on that occasion, because it wasn't really possible to go out and because of fear. I told Pero Karajica, the priest, and the nuns, that if they were afraid, if they couldn't face up to the situation, I told them they were free, that they didn't have any obligations. And then they asked me, "What will you do?" I said, "I'll stay on here. I'll be here." But I was convinced that the situation was a temporary one after all and that the situation would improve. But when they saw that I had decided to remain there, after they'd been called by the people who were fleeing, et cetera, after all these events, they decided to remain with me in the parish house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we're at the time for the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We have come to the break time. We shall resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecution to continue their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just as we broke for the recess, you told us that you had decided to stay in the parish church in Brajkovici. Can you tell us why you were prepared to stay.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: That was my main task. There was no way for me to know what would happen next. I just wanted to stay put. I didn't want to go into any other uncertainty. I didn't feel that there was any danger for me, and I just wanted to perform my duty. I wanted to stay in the place that I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the events that unfolded on the 8th of June, 1993 as Brajkovici came under attack.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I've already said that we could hear explosions before dawn, and then this increased. There was more shooting from small and big weapons. There were explosions, bursts of fire, and sometime around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning in that area I saw people moving, fleeing their homes. And then later on - I don't know when exactly, but it was probably around noon - a shell fell on the church tower, and later on another shell fell in the churchyard, in the L-shaped churchyard. This is where a shell fell. Some windowpanes were broken as a result of that. And then we residents of the parish church - myself, the chaplain, and two nuns and a anybody of ours who found shelter in the parish house - then decided to move to the staircase leading down to the basement. The walls were much thicker there. We decided to do that to protect ourselves from shelling. This situation didn't last too long. Then we heard banging on the entrance door. I was in my priest's uniform. I went to open the door. As I reached the end of the corridor, where is there is a little entrance hall and where the entrance to the parish house is - we're talking about a very small area of some 4 or 5 square metres - there was a burst of gunfire through the door. I was standing at -- some metres from the door, and the bullets ended up on the wall on my left side. Again, I could hear doors being kicked and some unknown men burst through the broken door into the building. They said, "How many of you are there? Give us the exact number. If you give us one more, we will kill you -- if you give us one less, we will kill you." I counted heads. I told them how many we were. They asked us to come out of the house. They lined us up against the wall. We were standing there for a while, and then a tall young man with dark hair and a dark band around the forehead asked another young man, who was sitting on the staircase, he was feeling -- he was embarrassed. He was covering his face. So this first guy asked the other guy and said, "What are these people like?" So this other young man said, "Well, they are good." And then we were escorted at the gunpoint to the house. I was taken by one person to the side of the house and the chaplain was taken to another side of the house. The house was searched. Nothing was found. There was nothing special in the house, just our affairs, our furniture, our things. We returned downstairs, and then we were ordered to abandon the parish office. I told them that we wished to stay. I asked them who the commander was. I wanted to talk to the commander. Then they sent a message to somebody -- and well, I repeated for three or four times that I wanted to speak to the commander, because we wanted to stay. And finally, while all this was happening, a man came riding a horse, and he was carrying a green flag with some Arabic inscriptions on it. He rode into our churchyard, and these men started saying, "Well, this is our sultan." I was not paying too much attention to that. I didn't feel concern. I was just insisting on us wanting to stay. However, an order was received that we should go. Our vehicles were taken away, and another vehicle was provided for us. Nobody told us where we were going. And then I asked the person who portrayed himself as being their boss, I asked him, "Can we go to the church, please?" We went to the church, and I told him, "This is a religious facility. This is church furniture. There are some paintings. Please don't let this become war booty. You should secure the place. I don't know you personally, but I think you should make sure that nothing is taken away from the church." He called a soldier and told him that nothing should be touched in the church. They gave us half an hour. We collected some personal belongings. And since there was no other vehicle to be provided for us, they decided to take our two cars, and in these two cars we went to Ovnak, in the direction of Zenica. This is about 500 or a kilometre to Ovnak, which is on the border between Zenica and Travnik. In our cars, there were soldiers who were escorting us. As we were driving, we were stopped several times. We were asked to get out of the cars, but our soldiers wouldn't allow that. We arrived in Ovnak. A car should have been waiting for us there; however, there was no car. There were a lot of troops there. There were vehicles, but all of them taken, so we could not change our transportation. And then a man appeared, a short man, who was recognised by Pero, and Pero told him, "Osman, where have you been?" Osman approached us; however, we had to leave the area quite soon. We didn't know what had happened. And this Osman, I'd seen him before. He is a very -- a poor man. He would come to Vlado Markovic, to Susanj. He would do some jobs for him, and he would be paid by Vlado Markovic. Later on we sat in our cars. Again, we were escorted, and we continued driving towards Zenica. We stopped in Pojske. We were accommodated in the old school there. We found some parishioners from Brajkovici there, some 30 or 40 men. There were children and women. There were elderly people. There was one disabled person. We were accommodated there, and we didn't know what would happen next. My --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, excuse me for interrupting, Witness, but I do have some questions about what you've just been telling us. You initially told us that when you were in the church, there was a neighbour that was with you. Do you recall her name?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Ana Matosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names or identities of any of the soldiers who entered the Brajkovici parish church?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I don't know. They all spoke Croatian or Bosniak. I could understand them. But I did not know any of them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Some of them wore camouflage uniforms. Some of them wore a combination of camouflage uniform and civilian clothes. So they wore all sorts of things. They told us that they were Mujahedins. That's what they told us. That's how they referred to themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long, Witness, did you remain in Pojske on that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: On that day, we stayed there for two to two and a half hours. I don't know exactly. But in any case, not longer than three hours. We stayed in that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time did you arrive at that school in Pojske?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It was sometime in the evening, between 6.00 and 7.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go when you departed Pojske?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: From Pojske, we were escorted in our own vehicles, because they couldn't find any other vehicle. A short man with a beard told us to get into our own cars and follow him. The car that we followed was a greenish-yellowish Mercedes. So we started following him towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who was in the car that you were travelling in on that evening?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: In our cars, a Golf and a Hyundai, there was myself, the two nuns; and in the other car -- actually, one nun was with me and the other nun was with the chaplain. And there was also this woman. And in each car there was a soldier who was escorting us. So we took our parish vehicles, a Golf and a Hyundai. From the church, we took religious objects, the most sacred things we took with us. We didn't want to leave them behind. One of the nuns was carrying that as she was sitting in the car. And as we left Pojske, there was this car in front of us and we were sitting in the same order in our two cars, so there were no soldiers in the cars when we left Pojske. We followed the car that was in front of us, and that took us to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the school in Pojske, did you see any soldiers that you knew or recognised?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't recognise anybody. At one moment, two or three men came. One of them was short, sporting a beard. He was escorted by one or two other men. And we talked. He said to us, "You are not in a prison. You are free. You should be able to go to your home." Then I said, "Okay, if that is the case, there are children here, there are elderly people here. Then I think we should go to Zenica, find a bus there, a bus that would bring them back home." And then one of the escorts told me, "How can you, as a priest, abandon your community?" And then I told him, "Well, I'm here. I'm with them, at their disposal. But if what you're telling us is the truth, then I think that people should be returned." And then this short man with a beard hushed him and told him, "You shut up. It's not your place to say anything." And then he told us, "Okay, get into your cars and follow me." And then we followed him to the suburbs of Zenica, to the junction of roads towards Cajdras and Vitez. And there he told us, "Now you can proceed on your own. This is no longer a war area." And then I told him, "Okay, what if we are stopped? We have some of our own things, belongings. What should we tell them?" And then he said that his name was Nesib Talis. You just mention that name and you can go. And I said, "Where are we to go?" And he said, "Go to your parish office." And that's what we did. We returned to our parish house around 11.00 in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Nesib Talis is or was?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Later on he gave me permission to visit Brajkovici and Guca Gora. He introduced himself as the chief of security services of the MOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what the MOS stands for?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Give me a minute. I think that, like in Croats -- the Croats have HOS. I believe that MOS means a similar thing. That's at least my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you returned to the parish house around 11.00 in the night. Is that the parish house in Zenica or the parish house in Brajkovici?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: That's the parish house in Zenica, by the St. Ilija Church in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the parish house in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I stayed there for a bit over a year, between June 1993 and 11th July 1994. I was to take over the monastery in Guca Gora from General Alagic. And then on the 11th, together with Stjepan Radic and with a Theology Professor, Velimir Valjan, I went to negotiations Guca Gora together with the late General Alagic. And in those talks we reached an agreement on the takeover of the monastery. The monastery was in a very bad condition. Everything had been taken away. A lot of things were damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, again excuse me for interrupting, but I'll ask you questions about Guca Gora in just a moment. During the period from 8 June 1993 until 11 June 1994, were you living at the parish house in Zenica throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there all the time, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point during that period did you leave the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I would go to visit the parish in Brajkovici. That happened on several occasions -- quite often, actually. Not only the parish, but on those occasions I would also visit two houses where the remaining parishioners of the Brajkovici parish lived. One of the houses belonged to Lovro Simic. There were people there, some 30 or 40 of them under guard. And also, the other house was in Susanj, belonging to Zoran Markovic. There were some other detainees in that house, in a very confined space, also under guard. There may have been up to 65 of them there. That's where I would go, and later on, when we were aware of their existence, we would bring them humanitarian aid. I would also go to Guca Gora, and up there in Krpeljici village, I found 12 or 13 persons, elderly persons mostly. And then in Guca Gora there was a bedridden woman; her nickname was Puza. And she died in the meantime. That's the people that I found there. And on one or two occasions I was granted permit to go to Vitez, and I took the opportunity to do that. I can also say that I also went to Visoko, and later on, after Vares, after the war in Vares, I went to Vares, to the parish office there, for just one day. And I returned on that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the period from June 1993 through July 1994, did you have the opportunity to minister any of the parishioners in the Brajkovici parish?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: The only people that lived there lived in those two houses. When we went to Brajkovici parish, we would bring them humanitarian aid. We did not minister any parishioners. There was Konjevici village in the territory of Zenica. Some of the parishioners were there. On Sundays we would go and deliver the holy mass there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this, again, period June 1993 through July 1994, as you were travelling outside Zenica, did you see or observe anything unusual?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: On the third day after my arrival in Zenica, on the third or on the fourth day, I was asked to go and bury some dead bodies. I believe that a person called Mirsad, a member of the civilian protection from Zenica, organised it up there. I went to Ovnak, and there I buried 18 bodies in Ovnak. There should have been 19 or even more people, but in any case the number of persons I buried was 18. And later on I went through the villages. It was always under the police escort. Sometimes there were some other people with me. We inspected the condition of the village. We wanted to see whether there was anybody left behind. At the beginning, I started counting the houses that were torched. All the houses were plundered, damaged badly. And then we started counting the houses that were torched. Later on, we just abandoned that attempt because it was just pointless, because the number of the houses that were torched grew by the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us at the beginning of your testimony that you had been the guardian of the Guca Gora monastery during the 1980s or part thereof. Can you please describe in general terms the Guca Gora monastery for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: The monastery in Guca Gora was founded in 1856 and 1857. It was erected in the place where the medieval monastery existed in the Lasva Valley. It covered the entire area up to the fall of Bosnia in 1463. This old medieval monastery allegedly had a key or a stamp up to the beginning of the Second World War, when parties torched the monastery in Guca Gora. Throughout the period of its existence, the monastery of Guca Gora had a lot of cultural heritage; however, a lot of it was torched in 1945. It was also the seat of the classical Franciscan grammar school between 1886 and 1900. Then it was moved to Visoko, where it still exists today. During a short period of time, between 1983 and 1990, there was the graduate studies of theology. It possessed a lot of cultural heritage. There were professors there who spoke several languages. There were Franciscans who in Bosnia were known as doctors, who authored a lot of medical books. The first schools that were established in the area were established by the monastery. The monastery enjoyed quite a reputation in the whole region, regardless of the religious or ethnic divisions. It enjoyed a lot of trust with Bosniaks, Muslims. While I was in Guca Gora, a soldier asked me, "Why do people say what happened could happen elsewhere, not in Guca Gora?" I tried to emphasise the role of Guca Gora throughout history, and in a certain way it was open to all people, so the older generations still remember that and pass it on to younger generations, this role of Guca Gora as a place being open to everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that a lot of it was torched in 1945. Can you describe the physical condition of the Guca Gora monastery immediately prior to the war in Bosnia in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the war, in 1945 the church was renovated. It was in a good condition. The left wing of the monastery was renovated from 1956 to 1958. I don't know how many square metres that was, but maybe 5 or 6 hundred, something like that, perhaps even more. The monastery was suitable for living. It had amassed a lot of treasures, and it continued to do so up until the war in 1993. So we were the first to have a painters' colony there, just before the war, and that was the first painters' colony which was held in a religious institution in the former Yugoslavia, as far as I know. Quite a few paintings have remained there. There were old paintings too. There was archival material as well. There was a library consisting of 8 or 9 thousand books. Just before the war, there was also an organ. I obtained it from Germany, a second-hand classical organ, which we renovated. It had an electromagnetic transmission. So these items were also obtained. So the standard was quite high for our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the monastery at Guca Gora, did it consist of one building or more than one building?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: After 1945, well, the left wing was renovated and the eastern wing, the old monastery, it remained devastated - that's true - but it was intact as a building, so there were two buildings. The monastery consisted of two buildings, which were connected. There was the part that hadn't been renovated, where you have a heating room and secondary facilities. And there is a residential part of the monastery. And now the old part of the monastery is being renovated, which is the wing facing east.
