That's about 25 times 15 metres -- 25 by 15 metres, and it's on three floors. So that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period from June 1992 -- 1993, rather, from June 1993 until July 1994, did you visit the monastery in Guca Gora prior to the time that you took it over from General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I went there on several occasions. I was escorted by the police. Sometimes I was able to inspect it in greater detail. The second time I wasn't able to inspect it in such detail. On one occasion I had to go to some village to get a permit there, but I went there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the condition of the monastery during those times when you visited it.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, to my first visits I was able to see that the monastery had been completely devastated. Its possessions, its furniture was missing. I noticed that the library was still there, in a sort of reception room, in the guardian's reception room, which is where I spent a lot of time. I noticed that there were troops there. There were blankets on the floor. In one part they would dry barley, and I noticed a biblical dictionary in one part, and I said I would like to take it, and they allowed me to do so. I took it with me to Zenica. But as far as I could tell, I didn't see any furniture on the premises, any other things that were formally in the monastery. It had been devastated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate for us what you mean by "devastated," and give us concrete, specific examples of what you mean by "devastated."

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, there were -- the troops were there. There was writing on the walls. There were picture that had been put up on the walls on the guardian's premises, not very decent pictures. The command was there, as I had said. Our furniture wasn't there, our equipment wasn't there. Everything was missing. Everything that was formerly in the monastery was missing. The television wasn't there. None of the equipment, none of the furniture was there. There was nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, what any of the writing on the walls said? Or can you describe the writing on the walls?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, I saw new things on each occasion. I saw inscriptions in Arabic on one of the doors. There were inscriptions in several languages: In Italian, French, and in Arabic, I think. And on each occasion, I discovered new things. And when I took over the church, I discovered that there were writings in the church. It said "Allah-U-Ekber," one had signed on a column later on. When I took charge of the monastery, the first and last name of this person had been written down there. Later I found out that a fresco by Zlatko Keser from Zagreb had been seriously damaged. It had been painted in the 1980s. It was about 30 or 40 square metres large. It had been splattered with some sort of colour. And another cultural object, artistic object had been damaged. That was even Dulcic's fresco, a painter from Dubrovnik. Benches had been broken. The church was a mess. There were inscriptions on the altar. Paint had been poured over that area. It was in a mess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that there were some pictures, as you put it, not very decent pictures. What kind of pictures did you see had been put up?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, the sort of thing that young people usually put up, fairly liberal pictures from magazines that had been put up on the walls. That was in a part where the troops were. I saw that in the guardian's office part of the monastery, and I also saw messages that had been written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On any of these occasions when you visited the monastery prior to taking possession from General Alagic, did you have an opportunity to observe the organ in the monastery?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: During my first visits, I wasn't able to see the organ. During one of those visits, I noticed that the organ was missing and that there were many magazines at the site where the organ used to be. A lot of magazines had been piled up from the library.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever on any other occasion see the organ that you had purchased in Germany for the monastery?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: From the time I visited the monastery until the time I took it over, no, I never saw the organ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber anything that might have happened to the library that was in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: When I took charge of the monastery, when I took it over from General Alagic, that was the 11th -- on the 11th of December, 1994, we inspected the premises in greater detail and organised a commission that was supposed to make a list of the things that were in the monastery and the things that were missing. But the commission didn't want to make a list of everything we said. They wouldn't put -- they wouldn't note down that certain items of furniture had been there. They said they didn't know that. So I said, "Okay, well, state that there was no furniture in the monastery." But the library was there. I noticed that some people had taken some books away, given some books to others. But on the whole, the library was still intact just before I took charge of the place. On the day we took charge of the place, the library had disappeared. I then told General Alagic that the books should be returned. He said that in three or four days I'd be able to see the library and it would be returned. Unfortunately, that was never done while I was there. I later searched for the library. Some individuals would bring in some books. Some people wanted favours in return and wanted me to pay for books, but I discovered that a significant part of library had been taken to a village above Turbe, to Karaula, to the school. I found out that that's where the library had been taken. And the director of the school - and by that time I had already taken charge of the monastery - when I exerted a little more pressure on the director, Mr. Halilovic brought some of those books to Guca Gora in a TAM, a vehicle. But that was later on, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what was the date that you took control of the monastery from General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I said on the 11th we went to negotiate, and on the following day we formed a commission to take over all of that and to make a list of the situation. On the 13th, I brought in workers from Zenica to carry out repair work, to work on the water supply, the electricity, because we didn't have any lights. I wanted this to be done in order to be able to take charge of the monastery. So after these repairs had been done about -- on about the 12th of September I was able to move into the monastery, which is what I did. Up until that time, the troops guarded that monastery. And once I had moved in, they also protected the people in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you moved into the monastery on the 12th of September of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the date that you entered into discussions with General Alagic was what date?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It was on the 11th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the times prior to meeting with General Alagic on the occasions when you were at the monastery, did you notice any damage to the external parts of the monastery or any objects on the grounds of the monastery?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, some of the windows had been broken, some of the doors had been broken. The walls were intact. The contents of the monastery had either been destroyed or taken out, such as the benches in the church. People put fires in various places when heating was necessary, and then they would make -- improvise chimneys. They would arrange the premises according to their needs. So this is the damage that had been done. But it wasn't destroyed. Later the roof of the entire church had to be repaired, replaced, and part of the monastery had to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Defence takes the floor, I would like to ask you some questions that concern your answers to the Prosecution's questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I'd like to go back to 1992, which is when you said that you noticed foreign elements arriving in the region, in the area. The Prosecution asked you to be more specific and to say who these foreign elements were, and you said that as far as you knew, they called them the Mujahedin and that some of them came from other countries. The Trial Chamber would like to know, in light of your testimony, when the Mujahedin arrived, did they arrive as civilians or as troops, as military men? Were these people civilians or tourists or people who came to act as soldiers? What was their status?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, they were dressed in a particular way. In our area, they were wearing a special sort of clothing, some sort of cloaks or scarves around their heads and necks. They had long beards. Sometimes they had parts of camouflage uniforms on them, a jacket of some kind, things like that. I met them later, too, in Guca Gora. When I took over there, there were many of them in Guca Gora. And Abu Hamza, the notorious Abu Hamza was there too - it's a function rather than his real name - and he founded a mosque in Guca Gora and gathered some people in Guca Gora. So I met some people there. I had some unpleasant experiences too. Once when I was travelling from Zenica with a Muslim worker and a nun behind the Maljine village, that's north from Guca Gora, about two kilometres from there, I met him on the road because there was a van full of Mujahedin going in the same direction towards Guca Gora as I was. And they obstructed the road. One approached us with a weapon. He was about 30 metres from the car and pointed his weapon at the car, and we were wondering what to do. There was nothing for us to do. That's what the situation was. I heard people speaking in the van. I heard a language that I didn't understand. He then returned to the van, and they continued for about 100, 150 metres, and a man came out of the vehicle and later he entered a house in the village, in Maljine. That's the part that is mostly inhabited by Muslims, by Bosniaks. I know that house even today. It seems it was a man from that house. I didn't know him personally, but I saw him. He was dressed differently then. So when they advanced, I decided that we would go to Guca Gora. We continued on, and I went there with a worker to fix the water supply. So I met them on many occasions, and on that second occasion they obstructed our passage in Guca Gora and started blackmailing us. So throughout that period of time, from 1994, when I took charge of the monastery, I think that the first inhabitants returned towards 1998 to Guca Gora, about 10 or 11 families perhaps. And in 1999, I think that's when they started withdrawing, that's when they started leaving. So throughout that period of time, I had both pleasant and unpleasant meetings with them. There were interventions in the monastery. On one occasion, they came to visit the church. I think it was in 1994 or 1995. I'm not quite sure now. And the people who were protecting the church, the BH army members, they asked me what we should do. Are we going to let them in? It would be embarrassing not to let them in. I told them to let them in, and we went into the church so that they could visit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't answered my question precisely. When they arrived in 1992, what the Trial Chamber wants to know is what their status was. Were they soldiers or were they civilians? According to what you were told and what you saw, when they arrived in camouflage or military uniforms, were they civilians or soldiers? Were they under someone's command?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: When I first met them, they weren't wearing the civilian clothes that people from that area usually wore, and they weren't wearing those uniforms that ended up being the camouflage uniforms of the army either. They were wearing Arabic clothing of their own, and later on they would take elements of military uniforms. But they did have weapons; that is for sure. I would always see them carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But on their civilian clothes or military clothes, were there any insignia? Were there any distinctive signs or nothing at all? Did you notice insignia of any kind? Because you said that you had seen some of them occupying the monastery. Did they have insignia of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Apart from the particular clothes that they were wearing, I didn't notice any other insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question concerning the monastery: According to what you have told us, certain items went missing - for example, books - some damage was caused. But this damage, was it serious or minor? What would you say? How would you describe it? When, thanks to General Alagic, you were able to take over the monastery, was it in a terrible condition? Was it in a decent condition, an average condition? Was it -- had it been badly affected? How would you describe the premises when you took charge of them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the building as such had not been destroyed. There was no significant structural damage. But on the premises inside, there was damage. The doors, the windows had been damaged. The building as such had sustained minor damage, but inside the devastation was complete. It was a mess, a terrible mess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You also said that before 1992 there were Catholics, Muslims, and apparently at the time the citizens were worried, given the events unfolding in Croatia. And a while ago you said that after the monastery had been taken over, someone constructed a mosque. So the question is: The Muslims who were there, did they have a mosque in 1992 and before 1992? Because you said that they had a mosque built. Does that mean that there wasn't a mosque there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: In the village of Krpeljici, which is connected to the Guca Gora village, the Muslims had a mosque before the war. They regularly performed various rites there. And the Arabs, halfway between the monastery and the mosque in Krpeljici they didn't build a mosque, but some sort of a building. There was a rich person who built this. It was supposed to be a stable, and they arranged -- they adapted those premises and opened a mosque. That's what the Arabs did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when you say "the Arabs," are you referring to the foreign Arabs or the local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No, these were the foreign Arabs, who also forced the local Muslims to go to that mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now, because the Defence has some questions to ask you: You mentioned someone called Abu Hamza and you said that this was -- this referred to a position, rather than to someone in particular. Can you be more precise and say what you meant when you said that.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: He was the main commander, not only in Guca Gora but in a more extensive area, I think. There are many negative things that are tied to this name that happened later on. He was the main threat at the time, not just to the Muslims. I know that there were certain incidents, scenes. When young people gathered, he intervened, because that wasn't in accordance with the Sharia law, the Islamic rules. Young people were supposed to entertain themselves in a certain way and wear certain clothes. So he was a sort of negative phenomenon in that area and everyone feared him. He also committed acts of violence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Krizanac. My name is Edina Residovic and I am representing General Hadzihasanovic. I would like you to ask you to answer some of the questions -- I am going to put to you about things that you are personally aware of. I have heard your answers. This is not a question. It's a comment. I don't know whether it's appropriate or not. But we are now faced with an overall attitude towards Mujahedin, a general attitude towards Mujahedin. But I want you to tell us about the events in Central Bosnia that you are familiar with, and I think that you, just like myself, are not affected -- we are not affected by the fact that this term is used in a certain different way. You've already answered some of the questions put to you by my learned colleague from the Prosecution. At the beginning of the war in 1992, you were working as a priest in the Brajkovici parish; is that correct, Mr. Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that your parish was in the area between Travnik and Zenica and that it included parts of both of those municipalities and about ten villages in which the population was mainly Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we locate the village of Brajkovici more precisely, which is where your parish house was located, we could say it's about 20 or 23 kilometres to the east of Travnik and that it's about 14 kilometres west of Zenica and about 14 kilometres north of Vitez. Would that be the location more or less?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, after the JNA attack and the attack of Serbian forces against Bosnia and Herzegovina, your testimony was that the Muslim and Croatian population was expelled from Prijedor, Banja Luka, Kozarac, Kotor Varos areas that were under Serbian occupation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, that isn't what I testified, but that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I was thinking of the statement that you had previously given. It's correct to say that you didn't say that today, but you can confirm that this is correct; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These refugees arrived in Travnik and Zenica and the villages that were between these two Central Bosnia villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The refugees came to this area without any property. They had fled from that territory in order to save their lives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were serious problems of accommodation, so they were either provided with accommodation in refugee centres or with family members or in abandoned houses, houses abandoned by people who had left the area because of the war or because they were working abroad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, apart from one exception. There weren't really any abandoned houses. Perhaps someone had removed the houses. But the houses were occupied on the whole, and people would provide accommodation for these refugees. So it's true to say that this is how they were accommodated, but there weren't any abandoned houses at that time, because most of the people occupied their houses at the time, both the Muslims and the Croats. So the people who were already living there, they would take in refugees from Jajce, Prijedor, Banja Luka, and from the other places that they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is my next question: Towards the end of 1992, there was a new surge of refugees after the fall of Jajce, Kotor Varos, so a lot of them came from there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to those refugees, there were thousands upon thousands of people who arrived in Zenica from Eastern Bosnia, from Foca, Gorazde, Rogatica. And all these were areas that had been occupied by the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Probably. I'm not that familiar with that region. At least, not at that time. Later on I saw that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, it was published - and you may have heard; and if you did, please answer my question - that towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993 about -- several thousand of people would arrive in Zenica on a daily basis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It may be correct, but I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly how many people arrived and in what period. I heard that the refugees were coming, but I cannot confirm for a fact that what you are saying is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with the fact that some of the refugees from amongst the Croatian people tried to continue their refugee exodus and go towards other states, towards Croatia, Dalmatia; whereas, Bosniaks mostly remained in Travnik, Zenica, and in that area. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I don't know when I said that or where I said that; however, that may have been the situation. Bosniak Muslim population mostly remained in the area of Central Bosnia, and most of the Croatian population from Jajce and Kotor Varos tried to go towards Croatia and further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time, the population of Zenica and Travnik doubled; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an enormous increase in the number of people in those two towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that that period, coinciding with the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, was a time when the relationship between the HVO and the BH army deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No. That was between the Muslim, Bosniak people and the Croat people. As for these two institutions, they became prominent later on. But that's how people saw it on the ground, that there was a deterioration in the relation between Muslims and Croats. That's how people saw it in the area where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: North of your parish, on the slopes of Mount Vlasic, the highest mountain in that area, there were separation lines with the Serb forces, and this line stretched from Travnik to Zenica in the length of some 50 kilometres or so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, these lines were manned jointly, by the HVO and the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. However, they were separated. Ones held some parts and the others held other parts. Their lines did not actually touch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are probably familiar with the fact that due to the deterioration of the relationship in March 1993 in your area the Frankopan Brigade was established with the headquarters in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Believe me, at that time I was not aware of the existence of that brigade. My information says that it happened much later, after 1993. During that period of time, when tensions increased and when war started, I was completely encircled. I did not have telephone lines. So wouldn't be able to give you any details. I believe that what you're saying is true; some units were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your village, Brajkovici, Mr. Zarko Jandric was the commander of a company of that brigade. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Mr. Zarko Jandric? No, I'm not aware of that fact. I know Ivo Bajo. He was some sort of a commander at that time in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, you did have an opportunity to visit Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: In 1992 or 1993, I don't know whether I went there. In 1992, in autumn, I think we had a meeting up there, all the priests, and we talked about the cultural heritage. We talked about the protection of this cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said - and all of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina are aware of that - you said that the monastery in Guca Gora, in addition to being a religious object, also played a cultural role, a significant cultural role because the facility dates from mid-nineteenth century; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a facility that is on the list of cultural heritage of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that within the monastery there was the communication and operations centre of the Frankopan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably know that the HVO and the army clashed in the general area of Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Busovaca. Is it true that these clashes had a negative impact on the relationships in your parish?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're also aware of the fact that between the 16 and 20 April 1993 the HVO carried out a series of attacks on Muslim villages, Ahmici, Donja Veceriska. Those villages are some 15 kilometres from Brajkovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I have the English text in front of me. Can you repeat the names of these villages. I don't have them in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the Brajkovici parish, were you aware of the fact that between the 16th and the 20th of April, 1993 the HVO carried out attacks on--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. We have an objection by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection on relevance grounds, Mr. President, concerning HVO attacks. Again, potentially laying the groundwork for an improper tu quoque defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, you have noted the objection by the Prosecution regarding the HVO attacks. You can answer -- ask the question and ask the witness whether he has any knowledge of these attacks, whether he had information according to which the HVO carried out military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to be clear on the fact that the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic is not trying to engage in a tu quoque defence. My questions are relative to some information that the witness may have. But before I pursue this line of questioning, I would ask you something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanac, this is not your first appearance before this Honourable Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a Defence witness, you testified in the Kordic case; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the Prosecution asked you about the events which took place in the Lasva Valley and about the information you may have about the things that happened to Bosniaks in Ahmici, Vecerska and other surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I don't remember what questions I answered, but I do have information. I do have some knowledge about these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness is in a position to answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about military operations, because you probably do not know what happened, but I'm asking you this: Are you aware of the fact that the population of Ahmici, the Muslim population of Ahmici, had been attacked and that over 130 people were killed during that attack, among them 30 women and 11 children? Did you have that knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President. Attack on Ahmici has, in the Prosecution's submission, no relevance to the charges facing these accused in this trial. The Ahmici case has been litigated before this Tribunal, and the Prosecution position is that it's of no assistance to this Trial Chamber in determining the charges against these two accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are asking the witness questions about the events that he was aware of or not aware of and the testimony that he gave in the Kordic case. And can you ask the questions that you intended to ask, but in keeping with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence these questions can only go against the credibility of the witness or they have to be linked with the facts contained in the indictment. Having said that, you may pursue your line of questioning. The witness may be asked questions only according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. If you want to ask a question that does not arise from the examination-in-chief, then you have to ask for special permission from the Trial Chamber and you have to explain your motives for asking such a question. We may allow you to put a question, but we have to know what your goal is, because I don't know what your goal is. You have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said with regard to the first Prosecutor's objection, I would like to repeat that the behaviour of my client, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, commander of the 3rd Corps, which was on the sixth level of command ladder, depended on the overall situation in the entire area. Therefore, I believe that you have already allowed me that I can clarify some general issues in the interest of the defence, because defence does not only go against certain events, because my client was never present at any of these places. In order for us to understand why the army is in a certain place and what measures are taken by their commander, we have to be aware of the military and other situation in the area. I believe that in that sense you have already granted me leave to ask a few general questions, and that's why I did not raise the issue again and I didn't ask your permission again. Your Honour, I'm not going to dwell upon this issue long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber understands. The Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly the Prosecution would point the Chamber to Rule 90(H)(ii), in which the Defence is required to put the nature of their case to those witnesses appearing for the Prosecution. That's not at issue. The point here is that the Prosecution would submit that notwithstanding that Rule, the line of questioning which the Defence is seeking to put must be proper, in the sense that it cannot go beyond the issues that are at stake in this trial, nor can it raise a type of defence which the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has held is improper. While my learned colleague has indicated that she would like to ask questions about military and other situations in the area, that would certainly seem to be proper; however, if the scope of her question goes to massacres committed by HVO forces in other areas and which have been the subject of other litigation before this Tribunal, then that, in the Prosecution's submission, is a step too far, and that is the source of our objection. She certainly is entitled and, in fact, is required to put her case to the witness, but if her case, again, goes beyond the issues involved in this trial or raises an improper defence, then the Prosecution submits that that line of questioning should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 12.20. The Chamber is going to deliberate on this issue, and we're going to benefit from the upcoming break, and this will allow us to deliberate. We will return at twenty to 1.00, and then we will tell you whether you can continue with this line of questioning. Do you want to intervene on what has been said by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since you are going to deliberate on this, I'm repeating that the -- when discussing issues like this, the Defence sticks to Rule 90(H), in which it says I is cross-examination is what it is and that the witness may present evidence relevant for the cross-examination. In English it says "to the subject matter of that case." Military operations are the subject matter of this case, and I believe that the Trial Chamber fully appreciates that military operations that took place in that area may be the subject of the cross-examination, because they are an integral part of General Hadzihasanovic's defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I raise one small matter on behalf of Mr. Kubura, and that is that the charge in this case, one of the charges, is that there was wanton destruction not justified by military necessity. And in order to consider the potential defence of military necessity, it may be necessary to look at what attacks were conducted by various armed forces in the area to be able to consider the entire situation and determine whether military necessity is a defence in the circumstances. And for those reasons, there may be questions along these lines in the future by Mr. Kubura as well. That's why I raise it, even though we are not cross-examining at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You will have our decision at quarter to 1.00. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume. The Trial Chamber has deliberated, with regard to the matter raised by the Defence concerning the possibility, in accordance with the Rule 90, the possibility of asking the witness questions that have to do with matters with regard to which the Prosecution did not ask this witness questions. So the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that when the questions concern historical matters or political and military matters, in order to establish certain facts, certain events that took place, either before or after the facts that were the subject of the examination or concomitantly, the Defence, when presenting its case can summon any witness who could confirm or provide evidence that there were such facts. The witness can only testify about facts that he personally witnessed and cannot answer questions concerning facts that are things he knows by hearsay. To examine the witness about events -- alleged events in some other place, given that the witness was not present, would be tantamount to -- would not fall within the scope of Article 90(H)(i) -- 90(H)(i), (ii), (iii). So the objection raised by the Prosecution has been granted. So I'm only going to allow the Defence to cross-examine the witness about issues raised in the course of the examination-in-chief. Their objection has therefore been sustained. And as we have seen, we shouldn't try to get the witness or to have the witness confirm facts that he was not personally aware of -- or rather, if he only has hearsay knowledge about these facts and as a result are not admissible in this case. So I would like to inform the Defence that the question put to the witness is not an admissible question. You can carry on with your cross-examination, but you must focus on issues that were raised in the course of the Prosecution's examination-in-chief. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect for the Trial Chamber, I would just like to tell you that this is a matter of exceptional importance for the first case of pure command responsibility. And if we are not in a position to ask such questions, we're being prevented from answering the question as to whether the commander acted in accordance with what was possible. We can't answer the question as to whether the commander was reasonable and other questions that concern the position of a commander, according to Article 7(3). So we will provide a written submission and ask for the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision. And if it does not do so, we would like to lodge an appeal, be granted the right to lodge an appeal. Thank you very much. I will continue with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krizanac, I didn't ask questions about the crimes committed in Ahmici. It's not that I wanted to ask you about facts that you are not familiar with, as you weren't there. All I'm interested in is whether these events also had a an effect, an additional effect, on the fear that the population had for the possibility of retaliation.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now return to an issue raised by the President of the Trial Chamber. When you were talking about the foreigners that you saw in that area, you said that there were also conflicts within the local Bosniak population. Could you please tell me, are you aware of these foreigners caused problems for the local Muslim population? Are you aware of any arrests of members of the army by these foreigners? And were there any disputes about religion?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they intervened when the young people gathered. And I know that Muslims were faced with the question, because their interpretation of the Muslim faith was different from that of the local population. So this was an issue, and I'm aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like to go back to another matter. And you testified about this matter in the course of the examination-in-chief. At the Ovnak bend, Ovnak road, there was an HVO checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Whether that was a HVO checkpoint or not, I don't know. They were civilians at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armed civilians, armed Croatian civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I've asked you this, but I'll repeat the question. To the north of your parish, there were the lines facing the Serbian forces, and it was about 50 kilometres away. These lines were about 50 kilometres away. I think we mentioned this before the break.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, on the Vlasic mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army units that had to leave Zenica and go to their positions on Vlasic had to pass by the Ovnak bend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, there are other possibilities too. This is not the sole possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But one of the roads used to go up there is the Ovnak bend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that the matter of roads was of exceptional importance for the population of Central and Northern Bosnia, because without these roads supplies of food or supplies for the army could not be provided if the roads were blocked. So it was a matter of life and death. Is that correct? You said that at sometime in April 1993 you heard that there was a war in Zenica and then part of the brigade of -- part of the Jure Francetic Brigade, with its headquarters in Zenica, together with part of the population arrived in the area of your parish; is that correct? After the conflict, towards the end of May, some of the HVO soldiers from the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica and some of the population -- the Croatian population of Zenica arrived in the territory of your parish; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Well, all those people who arrived in the territory of my parish were in civilian clothes, were wearing civilian clothes. None of them had military equipment, army equipment. But as to who they were and who they belonged to, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware of the fact that about 200 HVO members remained--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to interrupt you there. I would like to point out to the Defence that at line 13, 13 07, 13 you told the witness, "You said in April 1993 --" the Francetic Brigade arrived, whose headquarters were in Zenica. That's not what the witness said. You're making him say something he never said. And furthermore, in his answer he says no. He says that the people who arrived were wearing civilian clothes. So you mustn't make the witness say something that he never said when posing a question. I just wanted to point this out. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was referring to what the witness said when the witness said that he heard that there was fighting in Zenica. The witness said that he heard shooting from the direction of Zenica. As part of the cross-examination, naturally I suggest certain questions to the -- I put certain questions to the witness so that he can confirm what I say. As he wasn't aware of this, he didn't confirm what I said in my question. I will proceed and bear your objection in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you weren't a direct witness of the events in the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there when those events happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to that event, according to your testimony today, you heard about this event from other people and you buried the bodies of the men who had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The burial took place a week after the event; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief you described in a lot of detail what had happened from the early morning hours on the 8th of June, 1993. And you said that you saw that something was burning in the direction of Guca Gora and Grahovcici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I said Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Guca Gora. You also saw some people arriving from Brajkovici and Grahovcici, and they said that there was a bad situation.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. These were the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the shelter that you were in in the parish house, you saw some soldiers. Would it be true to say that the soldiers told you that you had nothing to fear because they didn't kill civilians and priests?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: They didn't tell me that. They killed a dog that was in the vicinity, immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the parish office, you took some religious items and books with you and certain personal items as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way to Zenica, you could still hear sporadic fire from a distance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Less and less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that on your way you came across a lot of troops and they stopped you quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were escorting you prevented those troops from doing anything to you.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: From taking us out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that in the school in Pojske someone with a period spoke to you. My question is: At that time, were you in a position to notice that some of the army soldiers, the BH army soldiers, had beards?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I saw quite a lot of people who had beards, but I don't know who they belonged to. I didn't know who they belonged to at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reached Cajdras, you said the person who introduced himself as Nesib Talis said that you could now go freely, because it was no longer a combat zone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zenica, the respected Father Radic was surprised because he thought that you and the nuns had been killed.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was surprised. He was worried about us, because he heard there was fighting in our parish, which he had visited earlier on because of his own parishioners from Zenica who had taken refuge in Brajkovici and they had taken some food there from the international representatives. So he was surprised and worried and he didn't know what was happening to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment when he visited his parishioners from Zenica, in of them wanted to return; however, the buses were already ready to take them further towards Vitez and other visits; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: That is completely untrue. The buses were not ready to take his parishioners to some other areas, because buses could not get there. We had already been encircled completely. I said that in Pojske, where we were -- when we were in the school, that it was my proposal to this gentleman that we mentioned by the name of Nesib Talis that if people were free to return to Brajkovici that we should go to Zenica to find a bus there, to return them to Brajkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We may have been talking at cross-purposes. Since you mentioned that Stjepan Rajic in Brajkovici, my question was about that time, the beginning of May, when he came together with the UNPROFOR representatives in that area, and not the period we are talking about now, in June. Very well then, anyway. When you arrived in Zenica, you knew that on that day the HVO issued information according to which two priests - Franjo Rajic and Pero Karajica had been killed and that the nuns, Tihoslava and Isabela Puljic went missing. Are you aware this information was published?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know this was published. I didn't have the opportunity to hear that. I only heard that on the following day from people, people wanted to talk to me, representatives of the media from Zenica wanted to talk to me. I was not aware of the stories according to which we had been killed or not killed. Later on, subsequently, I did hear that there was news circulating around Zenica that we had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you -- fortunately you are alive today, so this was -- the news that was published was not true. You are also familiar with the fact that the -- it was published that the church in Brajkovici had been torched and that the monastery in Guca Gora had also been torched.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't aware of that. I only learnt that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Krizanac is the following: Is it true that the false and misleading propaganda was one of the factors that compounded the situation and instilled fear in the population?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not killed. The church in Brajkovici was not torched. The monastery in Guca Gora was not torched.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: That's correct. Neither the Brajkovici church nor the Guca Gora monastery were torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already said that you issued a statement about that on TV.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival in Zenica, you returned on several occasions to Brajkovici and to that general area. The first time you went there was a couple of days after the combat operations, after the burial of the 18 bodies in Susanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Ovnak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went up there together with the civilian protection from Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, the police and the civilian protection from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that the civilian protection was the organ which after the combat operations took charge of the area, to asanacija and carry out facilities.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I learnt from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Brajkovici, you saw that the village had been abandoned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw a house which was seriously damaged and some other houses for which you assumed that they had been plundered.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I have to add something to that. When I arrived at that burial in Ovnak - this is on the border between the municipalities of Travnik and Zenica - my task was to perform the rites. And then I asked to be allowed to go to the parish office to take some of my personal belongings from the house. I did not have the opportunity, since I was in the car, I didn't have the opportunity to inspect the situation. I only had the opportunity to inspect the interior of the parish house. I saw that things were scattered around, things in disarray. I found some of my belongings, took them, got into the car, and then returned to Zenica. I didn't go anywhere else from there, from the parish house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I would like to look up something in my papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the OTP, on page 4 of the B/C/S version, it says "one house was badly damaged." Does that mean that you were misunderstood by the investigator?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: What statement are you referring to? I don't remember having said that, not in those exact words. Can you -- and I don't find it that important a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Earlier this morning you said that you returned some ten days later and that every time when you went there, that you saw that the number of plundered and damaged houses on the rise, that their number is increasing by the day. You never saw people actually plundering these houses; you just saw the situation when you went there.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: On the contrary. I saw a number of persons who plundered those houses. I would come across them from Zenica to Brajkovici. I would see them pushing wheelbarrows loaded with stuff that they had plundered. I saw a number of persons. I saw them. Actually, in Guca Gora, when I visited this area that had been inhabited by Croats, during my first visit I came across an elderly person wearing a folk costume. On my second visit, this person was no longer from, and later on I learned that he had been killed. I saw some people escorted by the Zenica police who had come from some distant areas and I saw them plundering those houses, and I was even threatened that I should move away. I wore my priest's uniform. They recognised me. They knew exactly who I was, and they asked me to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in Zenica you were guaranteed full safety and freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Nobody gave me this guarantee explicitly. I don't know whether there was anybody in the position to give us that guarantee. We lived in fear in Zenica. On one occasion they took our car from our parish office. It was a jeep that was in a bad state of repair. There were three police officers, and there were Mujahedins and they took the car away. So nobody could give you such a hundred per cent guarantee. We were never ill-treated; I must say that. But nobody could give us a complete, a hundred per cent safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of days after the arrival in Zenica with Fra Stjepan, you were received by the municipal authorities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was received there. But I don't know after how many days upon my arrival in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipal authorities were actually the ones who established the commission with Zeljko Tadis, Franjo Krizanac, Pero Karajica, lawyer Bozo Markovic, representatives of the civilian protection and representatives of the MUP as its members. This commission on several occasions inspected the area and drafted several reports on the 12th of June, 20th of June about the condition that they encountered on the ground.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: This is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September you visited Guca Gora. You were escorted by the civilian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: What date was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September 1993.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were describing the monastery and its significance, you said that it played a significant role in the preservation of the cultural heritage, that there were a lot of valuables in the monastery. Is it true that already in December 1992 it was decided that the most important things of extreme value should be moved to Zagreb and that it was done at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a meeting, because there had already been shelling from Mount Vlasic. We were afraid that the monastery would be torched. We had some very negative experiences from the Second World War. So we decided that this -- the treasures should be moved to a safer place. Later on I did not have any opportunity to visit the place, but I know that the treasures -- some of the treasures, that is, some of the paintings, some of the things from the archives were moved from Guca Gora. The library remained in Guca Gora, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who was it who moved those treasures. Was that organised by the church or was it with the assistance of the Croatian Defence Council or municipal authorities of the then-Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know to this very day who did it. Later on all these treasures were returned to the monastery. But at that time I did not have any communication with the monastery, so I wouldn't be able to tell you who was in charge of moving the treasures from the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the most valuable things that you later on returned from Zagreb were not in the monastery during the June events, in the June military operations.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: I did not return those things from Zagreb. These things were in Vrgorac near Imotski, the parish office there. Some of the paintings, some of the archives were there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the library -- although some of the books were scattered, the library was still in the monastery when you visited it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: It was in the monastery until I took charge of the monastery on the 11th of July, 1994. I don't remember whether I had the opportunity to see the library when I visited the monastery first. However, it was there all the time, until the very moment that I took charge of the monastery in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up to July 1994 the library was in the monastery, and when you arrived, after the monastery had been repaired, then you realised that the library was missing.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: After the monastery had been repaired - and it lasted from July to September - when I came to move into the monastery, the library had been removed, and my question to General Alagic was to tell me where the library was. I told him the library was here and it's now missing. And then he told me that three days later I would be able to see the library.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified here that later on, from the archives of Central Bosnia, that part of the library was placed in the archives of Central Bosnia after the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: The archives?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not the archives but part of the library.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: No, no, nothing was placed in the archives. I heard that some of the books were to be found in the school in a village above Turbe, whose name I can't remember at this very moment. I have already mentioned that name, but I can't remember it at this moment. That's where the library was to be found. I called the principal of the school, and then he asked me how come I knew that, and I told him, "It doesn't really matter. I learnt it from some people from Travnik." And later on, after a certain period of time, one part of the library was returned by the head of the Travnik municipality, Alija Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just consult my papers. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: The name in the transcript is wrong. I don't -- it is not Jovic. It is Halilovic. I don't know whether his name is Alija, but in any case his last name is Halilovic, not Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to some questions that we have already discussed. You were a member of the commission that was established in Zenica municipality. You've confirmed that to us. As a priest and as a member of this commission, you provided information about the condition in this parish to various international organisations, civilian organs, and others; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. We would draft reports, and we would take them to the Red Cross, as far as I can remember. I don't know. I wouldn't say that we had some major contacts with the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zenica, you were engaged in humanitarian work, and you tried to help many of the wretched people who turned to you for help.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, as a priest and a church official, not for a single time did you put forward your position or turn to the organs of Herceg-Bosna about the crimes that involved crimes against the Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me to issue a statement to that effect. I did not feel the need to issue any statements. When the representatives of international organisations came to Zenica and when they tried to talk to all the religious officials from the general area of Travnik and Zenica, I was always in favour of meeting them and I was always in favour of putting forward proposals on our part. However, this never came true because Muftija Alibegovic [phoen], the Travnik Mufti, he was of the opinion that he did not have to talk to anybody. His objection was that if a bishop was going to be there, he wouldn't be there. I told him that a bishop represents a region and that it should not be a reason for us not to meet. In any case, we never met. So that would be more or less an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a religious official, you know that quite a lot of religious objects were damaged during the war.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are certainly aware of the fact that some of them -- most of them that were destroyed were the ones belonging to the Muslim -- Bosnian corpus of the population. This -- I'm quoting UNESCO data, but I also believe that you are aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that quite a lot of those religious facilities were destroyed. A lot of Muslim, Catholic, and Orthodox religious objects were destroyed. I don't know -- I don't know whether that -- whose was the majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you paid a visit to a number of monasteries in Visoko, Fojnica, Kraljeva Sutjeska, and Guca Gora, you're certainly aware of the fact that BH army invested a maximum effort to preserve and protect those objects so that they were not destroyed, because they considered them monuments of considerable value for entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: What I know is that those monasteries were not destroyed, the monastery in Fojnica was not destroyed. Now, who was protecting those monuments and how, I don't know. I suppose that there was protection. In Fojnica, two priests were killed in the very monastery by the army members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were tried and convicted.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were tried and convicted; however, they were pardoned very quickly and released, and that was something that is hard to explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Krizanac: You are -- during the conflict between the HVO and the army, you lost a brother and two cousins who were members of the HVO; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: My brother was not a member of the HVO. He was already retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said cousins.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: My cousins were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to express my condolences.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: A lot of people were killed. I don't want to talk about my family, not because I have things to hide or -- or that a clarification is needed, but this is something that I find really very hard to talk about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I would just like to express my condolences at your loss and I would like to thank you for having answered my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO KRIZANAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you very much. Mr. Dixon, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Mr. President, after the examination-in-chief, you put several questions to this witness in order to clarify some facts that were important for our defence, and for that reason Mr. Kubura's Defence does not have any questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The OTP, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I would like to thank you, Witness. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you for having come to The Hague to give your testimony at the request of the OTP and tell us about the facts that you witnessed. We wish you a safe journey back home. I am going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning towards the OTP to ask them whether they have a new witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't have a new witness at this stage; however, the witness will be available tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. At 13.40 we do not have any witnesses to examine. I would like to remind the Defence that until -- by tomorrow at 9.00 they have to send their observations to the Registry regarding the objections of the OTP. And we would like to hear from the Defence what their observations are by tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are going to be able to do that today by 5.00. We are going to send our response to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I thank you. Before taking our decision, we have to know what the position of the Defence is regarding the points that were raised by the OTP. Before adjourning for the day, I would like to tell both the parties that the Trial Chamber is trying to give both parties the opportunity to ask their questions and that these questions have to serve to prove -- to establish the truth, and we try to avoid questions which are not relevant. And I would like to signal to the parties that the Trial Chamber would -- knows the fact and that the -- especially if the witness has already testified. I would like to observe that we are going to inspect those facts that both the Defence and the OTP are in possession of these materials and that we will listen with attention to the testimonies, both the questions of the OTP and the questions of the Defence. Having said that, I would like to say that we will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00. But Madam Registrar reminds me that it is not going to be in this courtroom but in Courtroom III, so it's not going to be here, not the same place, but Courtroom III. I once again thank you. And I will see you all tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
